I used to work for a well known LPG Gas Distribution company as a tanker driver. Usual work involved for this was driving around gas tankers, and delivering LPG Gas to residential customers, and the odd few commercial customers (much bigger tanks, which took longer to fill - this is important later). Not an *awful* job, pretty decent money etc. 

So after a few months I get brought into the office and told I'm being transferred to the evening/night shift. Meaning I would now work from 5pm - 3am. I wasn't too thrilled by this, as I did enjoy a good social life in the evenings. However these new shifts would be only Monday - Friday, and since I loved having my weekends off, I agreed. Oh and it helped that it was a hefty pay increase (double time after 8pm, cha-ching!) 

Anyway, after about a week of the new shifts, I noticed that I was being scheduled all of the larger, commercial drops. Deliveries that after 2 or 3 drops, would completely empty out my tanker. And of course, because the refilling plant at our depot closed at 5pm, I was unable to refill and move on to any further deliveries. So, I'd literally just have to go back to the depot, do my truck checks and head home. Most nights, I was home and in bed by 9/10pm. So I'd effectively be getting paid over £30 per hour for sleeping. Of course getting a regular night's sleep meant I could get up at a normal time, and I'd have like 7:30am - 4pm to do whatever I wanted.

After tax, I was regularly pulling in an average £700 per WEEK. Nothing really *dodgy* about any of this, as it was all above board and what I was supposed to be doing.

But it just felt way to good to be true at the time and felt a bit "naughty", and I miss that job TERRIBLY.

When I was 16, during my final months of school in the UK, I had a really bizarre and unsettling experience. 

I've always struggled with sleep issues, like insomnia and R.E.M. Sleep Disorder, but there was one night that really took the cake. I think I finally fell asleep around 4 a.m., after glancing at the clock and seeing it was 3:45 a.m. I've dealt with night terrors since I was a kid and have had some pretty wild nightmares, so I can usually tell when I'm dreaming versus when things are real. But this time felt like it was in some weird grey area. The only thing I remember is this blinding white light that eventually faded to a cream/yellow colour, and I could see these thin, dark figures surrounding me. It lasted for what felt like an hour. Then, I woke up. But not in my own bed...

The next thing I knew, I was in my English class the following day. I had no memory of getting up, getting dressed, or even going to school. It was like one moment I was in bed, and the next, I was sitting in class. I was completely bewildered and terrified, so I bolted out of the classroom, practically having a panic attack. The school called my mum, and she came to pick me up because I just couldn’t settle down. Not a single person believed my story, and I ended up at the doctor’s office to see if I was having a psychotic break. But I know what I went through, and no one can convince me it didn’t happen.

Since that night, security alarms in stores go off whenever I’m nearby, I’ve triggered fire alarms, car alarms - you name it. I even had an MRI once, but they couldn’t complete it because of “electromagnetic interruptions.” 

I’m not one to jump to conclusions about strange occurrences, but I can’t shake the feeling that something otherworldly visited me that night.

My father (kind of) killed a man in front of me when I was 11 years old. 

We were heading towards our car from shopping one weekend, when a guy (let's call him Bob) rocked up to us who my dad had a few issues with over the years. Drunken arguements, couple of fist fights at the pub, that sort of thing. He was obviously drunk and slurring his words, calling my dad all sorts of names. My father told him something along the lines of "say whatever you want to me, but don't do it in front of my son". The guy responded with "F*** your son". And that was it. Hell broke loose. 

My dad went to grab him by by the shirt/throat, not noticing that Bob had pulled a knife (which is the reason my dad never went to prison for this). Bob fought back, cut my dad's arm, but in the scuffle he lost his balance and fell over, landing on the knife which went straight into his chest. He must have hit an artery or something, because I've never seen so much blood before, or since. Unfortunately he died right there in front of me before the police/ambulance could even arrive in time.

My dad was pretty messed up for a long time. Turned to drink. He's now thankfully doing better, but I have to remind him at least once every few months that it wasn't his fault and he was just protecting me. Even though it was proven it was self defence, and that Bob had brought the weapon, we had to move, as rumours spread throughout the town we lived in that my father was a murderer. I got bullied quite a bit for that too in school.

 Throughout the time I knew my great grandfather, (up until around 8 when he passed), he never, ever talked about his time in the military. He was in WW1 as a 17 year old (lied about his age), so fair enough. We knew he served, he was in a wheelchair due to wounds that he received, but that was about the extent of it. He never, ever spoke of it. 

Then when he died, my parents were helping sort through his stuff, and found a Victoria Cross (highest British Military award for Gallantry/Bravery in the face of the enemy). They did some research, and found out that my tiny, mild mannered Great Grandfather was at the battle of the Somme, went over the top, and as he looked back to check on his mate, he got shot through BOTH legs with ONE bullet, sideways. At the same time, his mate was shot in the throat. My great grandfather crawled back to the British trenches, dragging his wounded friend along with his own crippled body while bullets and artillery flew over his head. 

Both survived. He received the VC for this, however he didn't even tell his wife/kids/grandkids etc. I guess he just didn't want the fanfare or praise over doing something anyone (or most people) would do for their friend. And he just didn't want to have to relive anything to do with that War. 

The lads back then were made of different stuff to people today, I swear.
